# Preface {.unnumbered}

These are field notes from poking R until the abstractions confessed, and then
asking what that confession is for.

The session that started them had no plan. It called `.Internal(inspect())`
on `NULL`, on `list()`, on a hand-built S3 object, on an environment, on
`bit64::integer64()`, on an S7 class, on an R6 generator, on a weak
reference. It pasted the dumps back into the file and argued with them in
the comments. The argument turned out to be an old one, wearing new syntax:
value against identity, signal against unwind, representation against type,
and the question of where a name is allowed to mean only one kind of thing.

::: {.epigraph}
R is a Lisp-family language that sells a Fortran-ish value illusion. Almost
everything behaves like an immutable value, with the copy postponed until a
write has to happen. A few objects refuse the illusion, and those are the
ones whose identity is part of the API.
:::

That sentence organizes the metal. The sentence that organizes the work you
do *with* the metal is shorter, and it showed up later in the same
conversation, once the dumps had stopped being the point:

> Name it. Admit only valid values under that name. Show it well. Extend it
> with verbs.

Object-oriented or functional is a choice of machinery under that law. The
data you have to represent drives the names. Functions compose the workflows
the data flows through. Everything else in this book is a consequence, a
source, or a place the consequence gets sharp.

## What kind of claim this is

Four registers, and they are not interchangeable.

A **mechanism** is something a manual or the R sources state. The claim that
there is exactly one `NILSXP`, `R_NilValue`, is a mechanism. It lives in
[R Internals](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html)
for R 4.6.1, and the initialization in
[`memory.c`](https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/trunk/src/main/memory.c)
is blunt about it: that node has to be the first cons cell allocated, or
armageddon happens.

A **probe** is something a session actually printed. `identical(NULL, c())`
is `TRUE`. `identical(NULL, list())` is `FALSE`. An S7 instance changed
address across `@p <-`. Those are facts about a session, and the small
[verification script](https://github.com/jimbrig/the-value-illusion/blob/main/verification/check-claims.R)
re-checks the ones that do not depend on a particular IDE.

A **reading** is an interpretation that the mechanism and the probe support.
"Empty `list()` is a zero of the generic-vector type, and that fact is older
and deeper than S3 dispatch" is a reading. It can be argued with.

A **recommendation** is a way to build. "A client is a handle; a config is a
value" is a recommendation. It is earned by the reading, and it can be
overruled for a stated reason.

The chapters mix the four on purpose. When a sentence is doing one of them,
it should be possible to tell. The [inquiry ledger](open-questions.qmd) is
where a reading is still soft.

## What this is next to

The design manual for the type-driven half of this taste already exists, and
this book does not pretend to replace it:
[S7 Design Notes](https://docs.jimbrig.com/s7-design-notes/). That book asks
what knowledge a model can carry so the rest of the program stops
rediscovering it. This one asks what the runtime is already carrying, and
which design habits are a truce with that runtime rather than a fight with
it.

[Advanced R](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/) remains the best long-form map of
names and values, environments, object systems, and conditions. [R
Internals](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html) is
the document these notes keep going back to, with the warning printed in the
manual itself: it is a work in progress and should be checked against the
source. Where the two disagree with a dump, the dump wins for that session
and the source wins for the mechanism.

## How to read

Read [The Law](00-the-law.qmd) if you read one chapter. It is the whole
argument in miniature.

The metal chapters are a guided decoding of `inspect` output: the header,
the three different empties, cons cells against generic vectors, the
machinery under copy-on-modify, the SEXP types you only meet in the right
context, and the condition system people keep using as if it were Java.

The hybrid chapters are historical, with the romance scraped off. R was
built for a conversation with data. That is why the REPL is so good, and why
a production package has to impose contracts the language will not impose
for you.

The taste chapters are the part that should change how a package is shaped:
open verbs, where state is allowed to live, runtime types as a substitute
for a missing schema layer, presentation as part of the contract, and the
data-driven close.

The [lab notebook](lab.qmd) walks the original probes in order, including the
hypothesis that did not survive the next call. That failure is the best
thing in the file.

Private chat is not evidence here. The probes, the manuals, and the papers
are. Where a conclusion is the author's taste, it is labeled as taste.
